title: The Build-Operate-Advise model: how internal AI teams actually reach production
linkedinPost:
89% of companies say their AI investments haven't delivered. The operating model is the bottleneck — not the model.

Most internal AI teams are built like software delivery teams. They build. They ship. They move on.

But AI in production is not a project. It is an operating function. The team design that gets you to a demo is not the team design that gets you to a system that actually changes how work gets done.

The Build-Operate-Advise model fixes the structural gap:

• Build: accountable for production-ready systems
• Operate: accountable for monitoring, retraining, incident response — and for EU AI Act Article logging obligations (fully in force 2 August 2026)
• Advise: accountable for translating outputs into business decisions and tracking revenue per employee movement

Only 27% of organisations have fully embedded AI across business units (PwC, 2026). The 73% who haven't have the same structural failure: AI capability with no integration accountability. The model works. The team around it doesn't.

What I would actually do:
• Map every AI team member to one function — Build, Operate, or Advise — and identify the function with no named owner
• Wire monitoring and retraining triggers into the build spec before go-live, not after the first production failure
• In financial services: treat Advise as a compliance role, not a soft skill. Someone must own the regulator explanation

Revenue per employee doesn't move from a working model. It moves from a model with an accountable Operate and Advise function behind it.

Full piece + the Build-Operate-Advise framework table — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What is the Build-Operate-Advise model for AI teams?

acceptedAnswer.text: The Build-Operate-Advise model divides internal AI team accountability into 3 distinct functions: Build (develop and deploy systems), Operate (monitor, maintain, and govern in production), and Advise (translate outputs into business decisions and measure impact). It prevents the most common AI programme failure: teams that ship models but have no accountability structure for what happens in production.

mainEntity.name: How do you structure an internal AI team in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: In regulated financial services, the internal AI team operating model must include a named Operate function with accountability for monitoring, incident response, and audit trail generation — these are EU AI Act and DORA requirements for high-risk and critical function AI systems. The Advise function must include someone able to explain system outputs to regulators and senior stakeholders. Build alone is insufficient.

mainEntity.name: What does the EU AI Act require from internal AI teams?

acceptedAnswer.text: For Annex III high-risk AI systems — including employment-related AI and AI affecting access to financial services — the EU AI Act (fully applicable from 2 August 2026) requires documented human oversight, activity logging, incident detection and reporting, and operational risk management through the system's lifecycle. These are Operate function requirements, not one-time build configurations.

mainEntity.name: How do you measure AI team performance using revenue per employee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Revenue per employee (RPE) is the correct business-level metric for internal AI team performance. The question for every AI initiative is: does this increase output without a proportional increase in headcount? Track RPE by function, not company-wide. Set RPE targets for each AI initiative before it receives a production budget. If the target is not measurable, the initiative has not been connected to business outcomes.
